question: When a supervised neural network fits atypical or incorrectly labeled training examples, is that memorization stored mainly in its final layers, in some other small set of layers, or in a small example-specific set of neurons distributed through the network; and can training deliberately confine it to removable neurons?

key_findings.claim: The paper's layer-level conclusion rests on three complementary but individually non-identifying interventions: gradient accounting, layer rewinding, and single-layer retraining.
key_findings.evidence: The core experiments train ResNet-9, ResNet-50, and ViT-small models on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and SVHN, usually with 10% uniformly randomized labels. Gradient norms estimate where examples influence updates; rewinding substitutes an earlier checkpoint for one final-model layer group; retraining resets one layer, freezes the remaining learned parameters, and trains the reset layer only on clean examples. These probes test influence, fragility, and functional redundancy respectively, not one common notion of where information is stored.

key_findings.claim: A small mislabeled subset exerts a disproportionately large and strongly opposing training signal across layers, but this does not itself locate stored memorization.
key_findings.evidence: For each layer the authors normalize clean- and noisy-subset gradient norms by the square root of the layer's parameter count. Although the noisy subset is only 10% of CIFAR-10, its aggregate norm is comparable to the 90% clean subset, implying roughly an order-of-magnitude larger contribution per noisy example under this aggregation. The average clean/noisy gradients have cosine similarity below -0.75 for most layers during much of epochs 10-30. Appendix Figures 10-14 extend the observation over training, noise fractions from 1% through 99%, three datasets, ResNet-9, ResNet-50, and ViT-small; the appendix explicitly says ViT results are not seed-averaged.

key_findings.claim: No fixed final layer or small layer set consistently controls memorized predictions under rewinding; the sensitive layer depends on architecture, dataset, noise rate, and rewind time.
key_findings.evidence: Replacing one final-model layer group with its weights from an earlier epoch produces heterogeneous clean/noisy accuracy changes. The main ResNet-9/CIFAR-10 Figure 3 and Appendix Figures 15-17 do not show a universal final-layer bottleneck across CIFAR-10, MNIST, SVHN, ResNet-9, ResNet-50, ViT-small, and 5%, 10%, or 20% noise. This contradicts a simple reading of prior claims that late layers alone memorize, while remaining compatible with redundant or distributed representations that tolerate a one-layer perturbation.

key_findings.claim: Many individual layers are functionally redundant for recovering noisy-label predictions, but the retraining result is deliberately only a one-way test of necessity.
key_findings.evidence: After resetting one layer to its initialization, freezing the other learned parameters, and training the reset layer only on clean examples, the model often recovers high accuracy on mislabeled examples that the retraining set never contains. This is evidence that the reset layer was not uniquely necessary to retain those predictions. The authors correctly note that failure to recover is inconclusive because optimization may not find a suitable solution. Appendix Figure 18 repeats the intervention over datasets and noise rates. The released implementation also updates BatchNorm running statistics during retraining, so the functional intervention changes state outside the nominally reset layer even while other learned parameters are frozen.

key_findings.claim: In the central noisy-label experiment, a greedy activation-removal search flips a mislabeled prediction after removing far fewer units than it needs for a clean prediction.
key_findings.evidence: For 1,000 clean and 1,000 noisy CIFAR-10 examples in ResNet-9, the paper iteratively zeroes the selected scalar activation in a linear layer or an entire channel in a convolutional layer until the candidate prediction changes. It averages model outputs over five Gaussian perturbations and reports the iteration statistic over 30 random training runs. The mean count is 5.1 for noisy examples versus 15.7 for clean examples, and more than 90% of noisy examples require fewer than ten removals. Selected units are dispersed over multiple layer groups for both populations. Counts separate mislabeled examples with AUC 0.89, compared with 0.87 for learning time and 0.93 for forgetting time.

anchors.section: 6.1 How many neurons, Equation and Figure 5

key_findings.claim: The critical-unit experiment identifies a small sufficient set for breaking a prediction, not a minimal, necessary, exclusive, or storage-specific memorization circuit.
key_findings.evidence: The greedy score maximizes candidate loss minus average population loss and repeatedly intervenes on the current network. Alternative correlated units may support the same prediction; a small adversarially sensitive cut set can exist even when the information is broadly encoded; and different examples can select different small sets. Moreover, the displayed objective labels an activation [z_l]^*_j but differentiates with respect to layer parameters theta_l and indexes the resulting gradient by j, without specifying the map from parameter-gradient coordinates to a scalar neuron or convolutional channel. Thus 'around 5 neurons' is a result for one operational perturbation on one core supervised setting, not a demonstrated universal storage cardinality.

key_findings.claim: Example-tied dropout can make the designated example-specific channels highly predictive during training yet largely disposable at evaluation in the reported small-image experiments.
key_findings.evidence: A fixed p_gen fraction of channels is active for every example, while each training example receives a fixed p_mem subset of the remaining channels; evaluation removes all p_mem channels. Table 1 reports clean/noisy/test accuracy changing from 99.9/99.3/79.3% to 90.8/3.1/82.7% on CIFAR-10, 100/100/99.0% to 99.2/0.1/99.3% on MNIST, and 99.9/99.6/89.5% to 95.8/1.4/89.6% on SVHN. Table 3 reports ordinary dropout and a sparse network retaining 99.5% and 99.8% noisy accuracy, respectively, while example-tied dropout reports 3.10% after removal.

key_findings.claim: The characterization of the dropout cost as a minor clean-example impact and a reduced generalization gap requires qualification.
key_findings.evidence: CIFAR-10 clean training accuracy falls by 9.1 percentage points, from 99.9% to 90.8%, while test accuracy rises 3.4 points; on SVHN the clean drop is 4.1 points and test rises 0.1, and on MNIST the clean drop is 0.8 and test rises 0.3. Part of the smaller train-test gap is therefore mechanically caused by lowering training accuracy, not by improving test accuracy. Figure 7 shows ambiguous, unusual, and possibly mislabeled clean examples among those lost, emphasizing that removable 'memorization' includes valid tail examples. No uncertainty, seed count, statistical test, test-accuracy result for the dropout/sparse baselines, or matched active-computation analysis accompanies these tables.

key_findings.claim: The dropout tables contain an unresolved hyperparameter/result contradiction in the exact source.
key_findings.evidence: Table 3 explicitly labels example-tied dropout as p_gen=0.4 and p_mem=0.2 but gives 90.8% clean and 3.10% noisy accuracy. In Table 2, the p_mem=0.2, p_gen=0.4 cell is 91.7% and 3.4%; 90.8% and 3.1% instead appears at p_gen=0.3. Table 1 also reports 90.8% and 3.1% for CIFAR-10 without printing its p values. The discrepancy is present in the arXiv TeX source and is not merely extraction error.

key_findings.claim: The natural-atypical-example extension supports the layer-level story but does not validate the strongest neuron-count or example-tied-dropout conclusions outside artificial label noise.
key_findings.evidence: With no injected noise, examples below C-score 0.5 form memorized sets of roughly 5,000 MNIST and 1,000 CIFAR-10 items. Figures 8-9 and Appendix Figure 19 report analogous gradient, rewinding, and clean-only retraining behavior: atypical examples have disproportionate gradient contribution and remain predictable after some layers are reset and retrained using only typical examples. The section does not repeat the critical-unit count, detector comparison, or example-tied-dropout intervention, so the headline five-unit and removable-neuron results remain tied to the artificial-noise setup.

key_findings.claim: One transition sentence reverses the paper's own layer-localization conclusion.
key_findings.evidence: Section 6 opens by saying the preceding experiments show that 'it is not hard to localize' memorization to particular layers. The immediately preceding sections, the next question, Figure 5 discussion, abstract, and conclusion all say the opposite: localization to any particular few layers is hard. The source therefore contains a consequential missing-word or polarity typo, not an alternative supported result.

anchors.section: 6 Memorization by Individual Neurons, opening paragraph

key_findings.claim: The released artifact is an incomplete research snapshot and cannot reproduce the paper's headline example-tied-dropout result from its documented entry points.
key_findings.evidence: At GitHub commit b09ba96e412c03301ddd0b944b511495d863c60b, the 27-file repository has six commits and describes itself as under construction. README commands name three nonexistent experiment files; no configs, results, checkpoints, tests, CI, lockfile, or license are present; data and plotting code contain author-machine paths; and modern PyYAML rejects params.py's yaml.load call without a Loader. More decisively, models.py's ResNet9_dropout.get_dropout has the ExampleTiedDropout return commented out and returns nn.Dropout, while the root get_model factory has no *_drop mappings despite CLI choices. A separate custom ResNet implementation calls ExampleTiedDropout but is not wired into the factory or a supplied training launcher. Its per-example mask is an unregistered plain tensor, hard-codes max_id=60000 and .cuda(), and is not preserved in state_dict. Syntax compilation succeeds, but a clean checkout supplies no runnable path or data products for Tables 1-3.

method.core_idea: Triangulate the location of supervised memorization with layerwise training signals, causal checkpoint substitutions, functional retraining, and fine-grained activation removal; then exploit the apparent fine-grained sparsity by assigning every training example a stable subset of channels that can be removed at evaluation.
method.mechanism: The paper partitions examples into typical/clean and memorized/noisy sets. It compares their normalized per-layer gradient norms and directions, replaces one layer group in a converged network with earlier weights, and resets/retrains one layer only on clean examples. At a finer level it greedily chooses an activation or channel whose removal raises a candidate example's loss while limiting population-loss damage, averaging predictions over Gaussian perturbations. Example-tied dropout then keeps a shared p_gen channel pool active for all inputs and chooses a deterministic p_mem pool keyed by training-example identity; only the shared pool remains at test time.
assumptions: Correct prediction of a uniformly mislabeled example is treated as unambiguous memorization, while low C-score serves as an approximate natural-atypical memorization label.
Layerwise gradient magnitude and direction are informative about where learning pressure acts, though they are not a direct readout of information storage.
A one-layer rewind meaningfully removes the function learned by that layer without creating an uninterpretable off-trajectory hybrid.
Successful clean-only single-layer retraining shows redundancy, while failure is not evidence of necessity because the retraining optimization may fail.
Greedy loss-based unit removal is stable enough under five Gaussian perturbations to distinguish prediction-specific units from ordinary adversarial sensitivity.
Scalar linear activations and whole convolutional channels can be grouped under the word neuron despite their unequal dimensionality and causal effect.
Stable training-example identifiers, fixed finite datasets, and persistent per-example masks are available to example-tied dropout.
Removing the example-specific pool at evaluation measures useful separation of memorization from generalization even though it also removes correctly labeled atypical examples.

techniques.role: Separates clean- and memorized-subset gradients, normalizes their layer norms by parameter-count scale, and tracks clean/noisy cosine conflict.
Creates a hybrid final model by replacing one layer group with an earlier checkpoint and measures clean/noisy accuracy sensitivity.
Resets one layer, freezes the rest, and trains only on clean or typical examples to test whether memorized predictions can be recovered without seeing their examples.
Greedily zeros scalar activations or convolutional channels using a candidate-versus-population loss objective until a prediction flips.
Averages the candidate output over five Gaussian input perturbations to reduce exploitation of a single adversarial direction.
Routes every training example through shared channels plus a stable example-specific subset, then drops all example-specific channels at evaluation.
Uses an external bootstrapped leave-one-out C-score threshold to select naturally atypical examples without injected label noise.

evaluations.setting: ResNet-9 on CIFAR-10 with 10% uniformly random label noise; 50-epoch one-cycle SGD schedule
evaluations.metric: Normalized layerwise gradient norms and clean/noisy gradient cosine
evaluations.result: The 10% noisy subset has aggregate gradient norm comparable to the 90% clean subset; clean/noisy cosine remains below -0.75 across layers for much of the epoch-10-to-30 memorization interval.
evaluations.baseline: Clean subset, total gradient, other epochs, and the same audit over 1%-99% noise in Appendix Figures 10-11.

evaluations.setting: ResNet-9, ResNet-50, and ViT-small on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and SVHN with 5%, 10%, or 20% label noise
evaluations.metric: Clean/noisy accuracy after independently rewinding each layer group
evaluations.result: No universal final layer is uniquely responsible; sensitive and redundant layer groups vary with model, dataset, noise, and rewind epoch.
evaluations.baseline: Unmodified final model and all alternative layer groups/checkpoint epochs in Figure 3 and Appendix Figures 15-17.

evaluations.setting: ResNet-9 across CIFAR-10, MNIST, and SVHN and several noise rates
evaluations.metric: Clean/noisy accuracy after resetting one layer and retraining it only on clean examples
evaluations.result: Many reset layers regain high noisy-example accuracy without seeing noisy examples, supporting redundancy but not identifying a unique storage layer.
evaluations.baseline: Initial post-reset accuracy, clean accuracy, and alternative reset layer groups in Figure 4 and Appendix Figure 18.

evaluations.setting: 1,000 clean and 1,000 noisy CIFAR-10 examples, ResNet-9, 10% label noise, 30 random training runs
evaluations.metric: Greedy unit removals to flip prediction and remaining population accuracy
evaluations.result: Mean removals are 5.1 noisy versus 15.7 clean; over 90% of noisy examples require fewer than ten; removing noisy-example units harms population accuracy less on average.
evaluations.baseline: Clean-example removal counts and clean-example post-removal population accuracy.

evaluations.setting: Mislabeled-example detection on CIFAR-10 with 10% artificial noise
evaluations.baseline: Learning time at 0.87 and forgetting time at 0.93.

evaluations.setting: Example-tied ResNet-9 on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and SVHN with 10% label noise
evaluations.metric: Clean/noisy/test accuracy before and after dropping the example-specific channel pool
evaluations.baseline: The same trained model before dropping its example-specific channels.

evaluations.result: Across p_mem in {0.1,0.2} and p_gen from 0.1 to 0.6, clean accuracy rises as the shared pool grows while residual noisy accuracy also rises; the printed p_gen=0.4,p_mem=0.2 cell is 91.7/3.4%.
evaluations.baseline: Twelve p_gen/p_mem combinations in Table 2; Table 3 contradictorily reports 90.8/3.10% for that same labeled combination.

evaluations.setting: CIFAR-10 ResNet-9 capacity-control comparison after 50 epochs
evaluations.result: Standard dropout p=0.4 gives 100/99.5%, sparse network s=0.4 gives 100/99.8%, and the labeled example-tied p_gen=0.4,p_mem=0.2 row gives 90.8/3.10% after removal.
evaluations.baseline: Ordinary dropout and a sparse network, without reported test accuracy or uncertainty.

evaluations.setting: No injected noise; C-score below 0.5 defines roughly 5,000 atypical MNIST and 1,000 atypical CIFAR-10 examples
evaluations.metric: Gradient contribution, rewind sensitivity, and atypical accuracy after clean-only layer retraining
evaluations.result: Atypical examples have disproportionate aggregate gradients, rewind effects remain dispersed, and reset layers can recover atypical predictions after training only on C-score-above-0.5 examples.
evaluations.baseline: Typical C-score-above-0.5 examples and alternative layer groups in Figures 8-9 and Appendix Figure 19.

limitations: The strongest unit-count and dropout evidence uses uniformly corrupted labels in small image classifiers; artificial label inconsistency is a precise proxy but not equivalent to natural long-tail, privacy, or verbatim memorization.
The natural-atypical section repeats only layerwise gradient, rewinding, and retraining analyses, not the five-unit statistic or example-tied dropout.
Gradient norms and cosines measure training influence, not the location or exclusivity of stored information.

A one-layer rewind creates an off-training-trajectory hybrid whose robustness can reflect redundancy, distributed coding, compensation, BatchNorm state, or layer scale rather than absence of information.
Clean-only layer retraining is asymmetric evidence and updates BatchNorm running statistics outside the nominally retrained parameter set.
The critical-unit objective is under-specified at the parameter-gradient-to-activation/channel mapping and the greedy result is neither a minimal-set proof nor a necessity test.
The term neuron conflates a scalar linear activation with a complete convolutional channel, so reported counts do not represent matched parameter count, information capacity, or FLOPs.
Main neuron-removal and example-tied-dropout results lack intervals, statistical tests, per-condition seed counts, and multiple-comparison control; Appendix says ViT results are single-seed.
The capacity controls report only clean/noisy training accuracy, not test performance, matched exact activation rates, runtime, memory, or equivalent hyperparameter tuning.

Example-tied dropout assumes stable example identities, finite indexed data, extra mask state, and repeated access; its operational cost and behavior for streaming, augmentation collisions, duplicates, or web-scale training are untested.
Dropping the example-specific pool removes correctly labeled ambiguous and rare examples as well as corrupted labels, which can erase useful tail knowledge.
The unlearning and privacy motivation is speculative: no membership-inference, extraction, certified deletion, influence-removal, retraining-equivalence, or machine-unlearning benchmark is run.
The paper does not report raw measurements or enough artifacts to independently recompute any figure or table from the released repository.
failure_modes: A distributed representation can have a tiny sufficient cut set for changing one output, so greedy removal may falsely look like sparse storage.
Different examples may rely on different five-unit sets; aggregating them can require a large fraction of the network even if every individual count is small.
Correlated or redundant units can make a genuinely involved layer appear dispensable under single-layer rewinding or retraining.
Rewinding a BatchNorm-containing layer without a matched activation/state calibration can cause scale and distribution shifts unrelated to memorization.

When the noisy subset has zero members in a minibatch or a high-noise setting leaves few clean examples, separate gradient accounting can become unstable or undefined; the paper does not document such batch handling.
Removing the memorization pool can lower the train-test gap by harming training accuracy, even when it does not improve generalization.
Stable example-specific routing can itself encode membership and may fail under deduplication, changed sample indexing, new data streams, or checkpoint restoration.
An example-specific mask saved outside state_dict can be lost on restart, making the trained function unrecoverable even if weights are checkpointed.
The released ResNet-9 dropout path silently uses ordinary dropout because the ExampleTiedDropout constructor is commented out, producing a plausible run that does not implement the paper's method.
The released model factory rejects all *_drop CLI choices, and README filenames do not exist, preventing the documented workflow before result reproduction begins.
Hard-coded CUDA calls, dataset paths, plotting roots, fixed max_id=60000, and unpinned dependencies make the artifact nonportable.
reusable_insights: Treat 'where is information stored?' as several distinct questions—where gradients act, which components are fragile, which components are necessary, and which small intervention sets are sufficient—and require convergence across them.
Report per-example and aggregate localization together: a small circuit per example can coexist with globally distributed storage.
For localization claims, compare sufficiency, necessity, specificity, minimality, and retained-task damage rather than equating any one ablation score with storage.
Subset gradient norms should be reported both as aggregate update vectors and per-example-scaled quantities; the distinction explains how a 10% group can match the remaining 90%.
When a training-time routing method is intended to enable removal, save routing state as registered checkpoint state and test exact restart equivalence.
A train-test-gap improvement should be decomposed into the change in train performance and the change in test performance.
Tail examples lost by a memorization intervention should be audited separately from mislabeled examples, because memorization can be useful for long-tail generalization.

A strong localization benchmark should include known injected ground-truth coordinates, post-hoc deletion, retraining equivalence, and unrelated-example specificity, anticipating the later INJ/DEL evaluation framework.
Source-level table cross-checks are necessary: matching method labels across tables exposed a p_gen/p_mem inconsistency invisible in the headline narrative.
open_questions: Does an exact or combinatorial search still find five-unit circuits, and how much overlap exists among critical sets across examples, seeds, layers, and classes?
Are selected units necessary under compensatory fine-tuning, or merely one of many sufficient adversarial cut sets?
How do results change when unit effects are normalized by channel width, parameter count, activation scale, FLOPs, or Fisher information?
Can natural atypical examples, duplicates, privacy canaries, and verbatim sequences be localized with the same critical-unit test and directed with the same training rule?
Does example-tied dropout pass membership inference, extraction, relearning, and exact retraining-from-scratch unlearning evaluations?
What is the union size and interference structure of per-example memorization channels over an entire dataset?
Can stable masks be generated from content or source identities without storing one mask per example, leaking membership, or mishandling near-duplicates?
What happens when example-specific routes are removed before rather than after optimization, and do shared parameters co-adapt to the memorization pool?
Would matched test accuracy, capacity, compute, and seed-controlled comparisons to standard dropout, sparse subnetworks, label-noise methods, and data filtering preserve the reported tradeoff?
Which values in Tables 1-3 are correct for p_gen=0.4 and p_mem=0.2, and which hyperparameters produced the headline CIFAR-10 row?
Can the authors release complete configs, raw metrics, checkpoints, environment locks, mask state, and an executable entry point for every figure and table?

competitive_landscape.title: Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization
competitive_landscape.difference: Zhang et al. establish that standard convolutional networks can fit randomized labels and that capacity or common regularizers alone do not explain generalization. The reviewed paper takes random-label fitting as its operational memorization probe and asks where the corresponding function is realized, adding interventions but not revisiting whether random-label and natural memorization share a mechanism.

competitive_landscape.title: A Closer Look at Memorization in Deep Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Arpit et al. show that networks learn shared simple patterns before noise and that tuned dropout can suppress fitting noise without sacrificing real-data generalization. The reviewed work localizes influence and proposes stable example-keyed dropout, but its ordinary-dropout comparison is much narrower and omits test performance.

competitive_landscape.title: What Neural Networks Memorize and Why: Discovering the Long Tail via Influence Estimation
competitive_landscape.difference: Feldman and Zhang estimate counterfactual sample memorization and influence through many subsampled retrainings and show that memorizing rare examples can help related test examples. The reviewed paper borrows the C-score approximation for its natural extension but operationalizes most evidence with incorrect labels and can discard the very useful tail examples highlighted by this predecessor.

competitive_landscape.title: Deep Learning Through the Lens of Example Difficulty
competitive_landscape.difference: Baldock et al. introduce effective prediction depth and synthesize the view that early layers generalize while later layers memorize. Maini et al. directly challenge a universal late-layer interpretation using rewinding and retraining, but their one-layer interventions do not rule out distributed late-stage geometry or a definition-dependent layer effect.

competitive_landscape.title: On the geometry of generalization and memorization in deep neural networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Stephenson et al. connect object-manifold radius and dimension to deeper-layer memorization and recover generalization by reverting final layers. The reviewed work broadens rewinding across models, datasets, and layer groups and finds no universal final-layer locus, but it does not reproduce the predecessor's geometric measurements or reconcile different layer grouping and memorization definitions.

competitive_landscape.title: Do Localization Methods Actually Localize Memorized Data in LLMs? A Tale of Two Benchmarks
competitive_landscape.difference: Chang, Thomason, and Jia introduce INJ, with known injected ground-truth weights, and DEL, which tests deletion of pretrained sequences, and find that successful methods still select neurons nonspecific to one sequence. This directly exposes what the reviewed critical-unit search lacks: ground-truth localization, sequence specificity, and a separation between deleting one behavior and locating exclusive storage.

competitive_landscape.title: Localizing Paragraph Memorization in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Stoehr et al. study extracted paragraphs, find larger gradients in lower layers, unlearn through high-gradient weights, localize one low-layer rare-token attention head, and perturb prefix tokens. It supports distributed influence but shows that layer conclusions depend on memorization type and architecture; it targets natural language recall rather than incorrect image labels.

competitive_landscape.title: Learnable Privacy Neurons Localization in Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: Chen et al. learn binary masks adversarially and report PII-specific neurons spread across LLM layers, then deactivate them for privacy mitigation. This resembles the reviewed sparse-across-layers conclusion in a privacy setting, but it optimizes masks rather than greedy activation cuts and evaluates PII rather than label inconsistency.

competitive_landscape.title: Finding NeMo: Localizing Neurons Responsible For Memorization in Diffusion Models
competitive_landscape.difference: NeMo localizes sample-specific cross-attention neurons in diffusion models and tests whether deactivation prevents training-image replication while preserving diversity. It extends the neuron-removal idea to generative leakage and sometimes reports a single responsible neuron, but uses model- and modality-specific generation evidence rather than supervised prediction flips.

competitive_landscape.title: Localizing Memorization in SSL Vision Encoders
competitive_landscape.difference: Wang et al. define label-free forward-pass LayerMem and UnitMem for self-supervised vision encoders, finding depth-increasing memorization but high-memorization units throughout the encoder and especially high values for atypical points. This partially reconciles deeper-layer trends with distributed units and covers unlabeled pretraining, whereas the reviewed probes require supervised labels and repeated interventions.

competitive_landscape.title: Memorization Sinks: Isolating Memorization during LLM Training
competitive_landscape.relationship: same-author scaled successor to example-tied dropout
competitive_landscape.difference: Ghosal, Maini, and Raghunathan show that natural-sequence memorization is mechanistically entangled under ordinary training and replace example-tied dropout with deterministic sequence-identified sink neurons protected from interference, scaling to 1.7B parameters and billion-token data. The successor narrows the original post-hoc localization premise, explicitly studies co-adaptation and learning-forgetting dynamics, and supplies a scalable on-the-fly mask design absent from the 2023 artifact.

competitive_landscape.title: Guess or Recall? Training CNNs to Classify and Localize Memorization in LLMs
competitive_landscape.difference: Dentan et al. show that many extractable continuations are guessed through language regularity rather than recalled and find different attention-localization patterns for lower-layer Guess and upper-layer Recall. This reinforces that a single memorized/non-memorized partition can mix mechanisms and limits transfer of the reviewed five-neuron conclusion beyond uniformly wrong labels.

competitive_landscape.title: Natively Unlearnable Large Language Models
competitive_landscape.difference: NULLs ties sparsely activated sinks to data sources, scales routing to roughly six million Wikipedia articles, and evaluates source removal against retraining, adversarial extraction, relearning, shared-fact preservation, and downstream capability. It operationalizes the deletion tests missing from example-tied dropout and routes by source rather than by every image, while requiring a modified model trained from scratch.

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim systematic evidence that supervised memorization is not confined to final or other particular layers, is often controlled by around five neurons or convolutional channels distributed across layers, and can be directed during training to an a priori removable pool through example-tied dropout.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The paper combines three layer probes over three architectures, three datasets, and several noise rates; adds a per-example greedy activation-removal statistic over 2,000 CIFAR-10 examples and 30 training runs; introduces example-keyed channel routing with results on CIFAR-10, MNIST, and SVHN; and partially extends the layer findings to low-C-score natural examples. Prior papers already established random-label fitting, easy-before-noise dynamics, long-tail memorization, effective prediction depth, and late-layer geometric effects, but the exact multi-probe layer audit plus example-tied routing combination was distinct at publication.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The defensible novelty is a useful experimental reframing: memorization localization is not a universal final-layer story, per-example predictions can have small dispersed sufficient cut sets, and stable example-conditioned training masks can make one designated pool disposable. The broader claim that memorization itself is stored in about five neurons is not established because the greedy cut is not a necessity, minimality, exclusivity, or information test and its activation/parameter objective is under-specified. The claimed clean removal is demonstrated mainly for incorrect image labels, sacrifices valid tail examples, and is not machine unlearning. Later INJ/DEL benchmarks reveal localization nonspecificity; later language, diffusion, and SSL work finds strongly definition- and modality-dependent locations; and same-author MemSinks/NULLs substantially strengthen the routing idea with natural sequences, scaling, co-adaptation analysis, persistent deterministic masks, extraction tests, and retraining comparisons. The 2023 artifact materially weakens reproducibility because the documented ResNet-9 code silently uses standard dropout and provides no complete experiment path.

reviewer_notes: Read and cross-checked all 22 pages of the pinned arXiv PDF, including every displayed equation, all 19 numbered figures, all three tables, both reference pages, and Appendix A-B through Figure 19. Visually inspected the rendered main gradient, rewinding, retraining, critical-unit, dropout, atypical-example, and appendix panels rather than relying only on extracted text. The cached extraction covers all 22 pages with no missing-text page. The official record remains arXiv v1 submitted 2023-07-18 and the work appears as ICML 2023, PMLR 202:23536-23557. Audited the exact official TeX/source archive, SHA-256 db87887f5df2951ff90146fe802d93465762455fd5ed96e2d5baeab83823d176; it contains the paper, bibliography/styles, and all figure assets but no experiment code, data, raw metrics, configs, or checkpoints. Source inspection confirms both the 'not hard' polarity error and the Table 2/Table 3 p_gen=0.4,p_mem=0.2 contradiction. Audited the linked GitHub artifact at current default commit b09ba96e412c03301ddd0b944b511495d863c60b (last commit 2023-10-26): 27 tracked files, six commits, no release environment, tests, CI, license, configs, checkpoints, or results. Python syntax compilation succeeds, but clean execution/reproduction does not: README experiment paths are wrong, data/plot paths are author-specific, yaml.load lacks a Loader, shell scripts assume missing checkpoints and GPU state, dropout CLI choices are absent from get_model, ResNet9_dropout returns nn.Dropout with ExampleTiedDropout commented out, and the separate custom ResNet path is not wired to a supplied runner. Checked 13 primary competitors and successors through current arXiv, OpenReview, PMLR, or official proceedings records on 2026-08-24, including the 2025 MemSinks successor and 2026 NULLs extension. No shared generated projection was rebuilt, and no repository file other than this claimed reading was authored.
